g.text: the planner aisleflow extends -- it wins two, loses two

text.style: font-weight: 700; font-size: 11.5px; font-family: 'DejaVu Sans', sans-serif; text-anchor: start; fill: #0b0b0b

g.text: Is aisleflow better? One cell per rival per map

text.style: font-size: 8.5px; font-family: 'DejaVu Sans', sans-serif; fill: #52514e

g.text: Each cell divides aisleflow's throughput by that rival's on that map, so 2.00x means aisleflow delivered twice as many tasks.

text.style: font-size: 8.5px; font-family: 'DejaVu Sans', sans-serif; fill: #52514e

g.text: Blue: aisleflow ahead. Red: aisleflow behind. Against all three published baselines it wins every cell, by 13x to 362x, and in 2 cells the baseline delivered nothing at all,

text.style: font-size: 8.5px; font-family: 'DejaVu Sans', sans-serif; fill: #52514e

g.text: because their space-time search keeps failing in dense traffic and a robot that cannot plan simply waits. Against the plain PIBT it extends it is ahead on the two

text.style: font-size: 8.5px; font-family: 'DejaVu Sans', sans-serif; fill: #52514e

g.text: aisle-constrained maps and behind on the two open ones -- congestion machinery pays where congestion is the constraint, and costs where it is not.
